name: Brandolini's Law
statement: The amount of energy needed to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than that needed to produce it.
meaning: Making a false or sloppy claim is cheap and fast; disproving it is expensive and slow. Falsehoods can therefore be generated far faster than any honest party can correct them.
mechanism: A bare assertion needs no support; a refutation needs evidence, context, reasoning, and a defence against objections, and the debunker, unlike the fabricator, must be accurate on every point or lose credibility. One person can emit many false claims in the time it takes to rebut a single one, and the simple falsehood is easier to grasp and remember than the complicated correction. The economics of effort run strongly against the truth.

examples.text: A fabricated health or election claim can be posted in seconds; a fact-checker must research, source, and publish a full correction over hours or days, and it reaches a smaller audience than the original ever did.

In debate, a speaker fires off many dubious claims in quick succession. Each rebuttal takes far longer than each assertion, so the format guarantees most claims go unanswered, and the audience reads 'unrebutted' as 'true'.
A viral rumour races across a network and is shared widely before anyone issues a correction; the correction then travels more slowly and reaches fewer people: the asymmetry playing out in real time.

variants.name: The Gish gallop
variants.text: The debate tactic that weaponises the asymmetry: overwhelm an opponent with a flood of individually weak claims that cannot all be answered in the time available. Named in 1994 by Eugenie Scott after the creationist Duane Gish.

variants.name: Swift's 'falsehood flies'
variants.text: The literary antecedent, from Jonathan Swift (1710): 'Falsehood flies, and truth comes limping after it; so that when men come to be undeceived, it is too late.'

variants.name: The firehose of falsehood
variants.text: A propaganda model named by the RAND Corporation (2016): high-volume, multi-channel, rapid, repetitive messaging with no regard for truth or consistency (the asymmetry industrialised).

whyItMatters: It explains why debunking feels like bailing out the sea, and why misinformation, propaganda, and bad-faith debate are so effective: the attacker's costs are trivial and the defender's are enormous. It reframes the fight against falsehood as a problem of asymmetric economics, not of simply 'being right'.

working.text: point-by-point rebuttal is the losing game the asymmetry is designed to win; triage to the claims that matter most and let the rest go.
'pre-bunking', warning people about a manipulation technique before they meet it, is cheaper than debunking each instance after it spreads.

working.lead: Raise the cost of producing nonsense
working.text: friction, provenance, and accountability on the supply side scale better than refutation on the demand side.

limits: It is an aphorism, not a measured law: the 'order of magnitude' is rhetorical, signalling 'far greater', not a calibrated ratio. Its main hazard is in reverse: the label 'bullshit' can be used to wave away genuine, good-faith criticism without engaging it, so invoking Brandolini's law to justify not responding can itself shield bad claims from scrutiny. It also presupposes that one side already knows which claims are the bullshit. It describes why debunking is hard; it offers no method for doing it, and can breed fatalism.
misreadings: It does not say refutation is impossible or pointless, nor that whoever asserts loudest is wrong. It describes an asymmetry of effort (that producing falsehood is cheap and refuting it is dear), which is an argument for choosing your battles and inoculating early, not for giving up on truth.
origin: Coined by the Italian software developer Alberto Brandolini, who stated it in January 2013. He has said he was inspired after reading Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow and then watching an Italian political talk show featuring the former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi and the journalist Marco Travaglio. It spread widely after a photo of a slide from his 2014 conference talk circulated online. The sentiment has older antecedents, notably Swift's 1710 line about falsehood flying.

sources.text: Brandolini's law, Wikipedia. — the canonical wording, the January 2013 origin, the Berlusconi/Travaglio trigger, and the Swift antecedent.
Gish gallop, Wikipedia. — the debate tactic that operationalises the asymmetry (coined 1994 by Eugenie Scott).
